newsitem.title: USA: WORLD BONDS -- European markets take center stage.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS -- European markets take center stage.

text.p: As prospects for an interest rate hike in the U.S. mount, portfolio managers are looking at European debt markets as a way to prop up return on fixed-income investments and keep mutual funds' profitable.
"I think there is value in Europe as a region," said Michael Perelstein, managing director at portfolio management firm MacKay Shields.
Analysts said the economic recovery in Europe, on average, is expected to be fairly muted, while the continent's unemployment rates remain at lofty levels.

Germany's jobless rate, for example, has been above 10 percent. And that, analysts said, is seen as the low end of the European scale because the average unemployment rate in Europe is currently around 11 to 12 percent.
In such a scenario, analysts said European central banks' next monetary policy moves are mostly expected to be towards lowering interest rates.
That offers a contrast to the United States, where the jobless rate is running at a seven-year low of 5.1 percent and concerns of an imminent hike are rampant.
"The most important positive argument for Europe is that central banks for the next year are in no mood to raise rates, unlike in the United States," Perelstein said.
"So you definitely have a lot of opportunities, particularly in the short to medium area of the yield curve in those markets," he added.
Experts said the higher yielding areas of Europe could present even better returns as inflation in those countries appears to have been tamed, representing no immediate threat for investors.
"Sweden, for example, used to be a high inflation area in Europe and it's now the low inflation center of Europe," Perelstein said.
"It used to have inflation rates of 7.0, 8.0 and 9.0 percent five years ago. Now it's running inflation below 1.0 percent. Even below Germany's," the portfolio manager added.
Perelstein said Swedish bond yields are currently trading around 200 basis points above corresponding German securities, while the country's inflation is about half a percentage point lower.
Italy was also painted as a low-inflation country where the fixed-income market shows some value nowadays.

"Italy's inflation rate over the last year alone has come down from 6.0 to 3.4 percent," Perelstein said. "So I think that within Europe, on balance, you still want to be tilted in favor of high yielding markets rather than the core ones."
Portfolio specialists said there might be a psychological factor working in favor of Italian bonds as well.
"Italy is seen as such a poorly run country that you get priced into bonds the fears of investors," said Claude Erb, director of fixed-income research at First Chicago Investment Management Co.
"(However), we think that Italy is not as well-run as the U.S., but it's not as poorly run as bonds are priced," Erb added.
Spain and Finland were also pointed by analysts as good investment options for those looking for value in the international fixed-income realm.
Among the places to be cautious about, analysts mentioned Latin American emerging markets and some areas of Asia, mainly the Japanese fixed-income market.

"I would say the bond people are still going into emerging debt markets," First Chicago's Erb said. "But we actually feel that those (markets) are kind of expensive ... They have pretty much priced in all the good news," he added.
Japan was also seen as a place to avoid.
Although many economists do not believe a rate hike is around the corner, they said the Japanese economy appears to have been moving on track.
"The economy will need the government to bridge demand, so there will be no immediate drop off in fiscal spending," Sanwa Bank Ltd said in a recent economic report.
"But the wheels of ... recovery have been given much needed lubrication in the form of a weaker yen," it added.

Analysts also said no major rally is expected in the country's fixed-income market in the near future. "The key story in my mind is the Japanese story, which is a great selling opportunity," said MacKay Shield's Perelstein.
